claims.claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) display striking differences in density of apoptotic neurons during the early postnatal period.
claims.source: Here, we report that the primary motor cortex (M1) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1), two adjacent but functionally distinct areas, display striking differences in density of apoptotic neurons during the early postnatal period.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Differences in rate of apoptosis between M1 and S1 negatively correlate with region-dependent levels of activity.
claims.source: These differences in rate of apoptosis negatively correlate with region-dependent levels of activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings showing higher activity in S1 than M1 (Figure 4) and lower apoptosis in S1 than M1 (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Disrupting electrical activity pharmacologically alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis.
claims.source: Disrupting this activity either pharmacologically or by electrical stimulation alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis and sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using 4-AP/0 Mg2+ and gabazine treatments (Figure 5) and kainate injections (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
claims.source: Disrupting this activity either pharmacologically or by electrical stimulation alters the spatial pattern of apoptosis and sensory deprivation leads to exacerbated amounts of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding functional area of the neocortex.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by whisker deafferentation experiments showing increased apoptosis in the corresponding barrel field (Figure 7B).

claims.claim: A first wave of apoptosis peaks at embryonic day (E) 14 in the rodent cortex and is believed to select the appropriate neural clones.
claims.source: A first wave of apoptosis, peaking at embryonic day (E) 14 in the rodent cortex, is believed to select the appropriate neural clones (Blaschke et al., 1996, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Blaschke et al.

claims.claim: A second surge of apoptosis affects the early postnatal cortex, triggering the loss of up to 50% of newly differentiated neurons.
claims.source: A second surge of apoptosis affects the early postnatal cortex, triggering the loss of up to 50% of newly differentiated neurons (Nikolić et al., 2013; Dekkers et al., 2013; Southwell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The death of developing neurons is mediated by the evolutionary conserved mitochondrial pathway.
claims.source: The death of developing neurons is mediated by the evolutionary conserved mitochondrial pathway (Shi, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi, 2001.

claims.claim: In the mammalian brain, the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway is highly regulated by proteins of the Bcl-2 family.
claims.source: In the mammalian brain, this intracellular pathway is highly regulated by proteins of the Bcl-2 family (Southwell et al., 2012; Ledonne et al., 2016; Nakamura et al., 2016; Shindler et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In the peripheral nervous system, neurotrophins represent the main pro-survival factors by activating the PI3K/Akt and Raf/MEK/ERK pathways, while inhibiting the JNK pathway.
claims.source: In the peripheral nervous system, neurotrophins represent the main pro-survival factors by activating the PI3K/Akt and Raf/MEK/ERK pathways, while inhibiting the JNK pathway (Kristiansen and Ham, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kristiansen and Ham, 2014.

claims.claim: The neurotrophic theory does not apply to the central nervous system.
claims.source: However, experiments using transgenic mice have shown that this so-called 'neurotrophic theory' does not apply to the central nervous system (Jones et al., 1994; Minichiello and Klein, 1996; Dekkers et al., 2013; Silos-Santiago et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple transgenic mouse studies.

claims.claim: In developing cortical neurons, the intracellular Akt/PI3K pathway is of particular importance to promote neuronal survival.
claims.source: In developing cortical neurons, the intracellular Akt/PI3K pathway is of particular importance to promote neuronal survival (Wagner-Golbs and Luhmann, 2012; Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Datta et al., 1997; Bittigau et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: An increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis.
claims.source: In general, an increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis whereas a reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis (Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Lebedeva et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis.
claims.source: In general, an increase in spontaneous activity is commonly associated with a decreased rate of apoptosis whereas a reduction of electrical activity exacerbates the number of central neurons undergoing apoptosis (Golbs et al., 2011; Murase et al., 2011; Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Lebedeva et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Transplantation studies with embryonic GABAergic interneuron populations suggest that both the extent and time point of cell death in cortical inhibitory neurons are intrinsically determined.
claims.source: On the other hand, transplantation studies with embryonic GABAergic interneuron populations suggest that both the extent and time point of cell death in cortical inhibitory neurons are intrinsically determined (Southwell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Southwell et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The overall rate of cell death in the developing mouse neocortex increases from P2 on, peaks around P5 to P6 and subsequently declines.
claims.source: In agreement with previous reports (Southwell et al., 2012; Verney et al., 2000), the overall rate of cell death in the developing mouse neocortex increases from P2 on, peaks around P5 to P6 and subsequently declines (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1; one-way ANOVA, R²=0.54, p=0.002, n = 38 mice).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis, as well as citations to previous reports.

claims.claim: Cell death at P5-7 almost exclusively affects GFAP-negative, neuronal cells.
claims.source: Cell death at this developmental stage almost exclusively affects GFAP-negative, neuronal cells (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The majority of aCasp3-positive neurons are GAD67-negative, glutamatergic neurons with a minor contribution of GAD67-positive, GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Southwell et al., 2012; Sahara et al., 2012), the majority of aCasp3-positive neurons are GAD67-negative, glutamatergic neurons with a minor contribution of GAD67-positive, GABAergic neurons (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 1C and D, and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) shows higher densities of aCasp3-positive cells (39.66 ± 14.93 aCasp3/mm²) compared to the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (15.51 ± 6.90 aCasp3/mm²) in flat-mounted sections.
claims.source: Most obviously, the primary motor cortex (M1) shows higher densities of aCasp3-positive cells (39.66 ± 14.93 aCasp3/mm²) compared to the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (15.51 ± 6.90 aCasp3/mm²; n = 3 mice), although the difference is not significant (t-test, p=0.28).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of flat-mounted sections, though the difference is not statistically significant.

claims.claim: In most cases, aCasp3-positive neurons are located in layer II at the border of layer I.
claims.source: In most cases, aCasp3-positive neurons are located in layer II at the border of layer I (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: aCasp3 labeling allows the detection of apoptotic neurons at various stages of morphological and nuclear degradation.
claims.source: Note that aCasp3 labeling allows the detection of apoptotic neurons at various stages of morphological and nuclear degradation.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from the immunohistochemical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Superficial cortical layers (layers I-IV) show a higher rate of cell death (29.31 ± 4.13 aCasp3/mm²) compared to deeper layers (layer V: 18.73 ± 1.61 aCasp3/mm²; layer VI: 6.76 ± 0.85 aCasp3/mm²).
claims.source: Quantification of the number of aCasp3-labeled neurons revealed a higher rate of cell death in superficial cortical layers (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1; layers I-IV: 29.31 ± 4.13 aCasp3/mm²) compared to deeper layers (layer V: 18.73 ± 1.61 aCasp3/mm²; layer VI; 6.76 ± 0.85 aCasp3/mm²; two-way ANOVA layer p=0.0002; post-hoc test sector a p<0.001, sectors b to f p>0.05; n = 11 mice).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Cell death is four times higher in M1 (sectors a/b: 57.76 ± 10.26 aCasp3/mm²) than in S1 (sectors c-f: 14.86 ± 1.52 aCasp3/mm²).
claims.source: Furthermore, cell death is four times higher in M1 (Figure 3A; sectors a/b: 57.76 ± 10.26 aCasp3/mm²) than in S1 (sectors c-f: 14.86 ± 1.52 aCasp3/mm²; t-test, p<0.0001)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In layer V, lower rates of cell death are detectable in M1 (sectors a/b: 13.79 ± 2.40 aCasp3/mm²) compared to S1 (sectors c-f: 29.97 ± 2.04 aCasp3/mm²).
claims.source: In layer V, lower rates of cell death are detectable in M1 (sectors a/b: 13.79 ± 2.40 aCasp3/mm²) compared to S1 (sectors c-f: 29.97 ± 2.04 aCasp3/mm²; t-test, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The deeper layer VI displays a low amount of apoptotic neurons and does not exhibit any area specificity.
claims.source: The deeper layer VI displays a low amount of apoptotic neurons and does not exhibit any area specificity (two-way ANOVA, sector p>0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of quantitative data.

claims.claim: The spatial pattern of cell death at P5-7 detected by aCasp3 immunohistochemistry was confirmed by TUNEL staining.
claims.source: The spatial pattern of cell death at P5-7 detected by aCasp3 immunohistochemistry was confirmed by TUNEL staining, which labels fragmented nuclei when cell death process is fully executed (Gavrieli et al., 1992). The pattern of TUNEL-positive neurons can be superimposed on the pattern of aCasp3-labeled neurons (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.001, detection method p=0.96, n = 3 animals)
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis, and a citation to the TUNEL method.

claims.claim: In P1-3 and P9-11 mice, the density of apoptotic neurons is very low and does not reveal any sector differences.
claims.source: In contrast to P5-7 mice, the density of apoptotic neurons detected in both P1-3 and P9-11 mice is very low and does not reveal any sector differences (two-way ANOVA, P1-3: sector p=0.48, n = 8 animals; P9-11: sector p=0.45, n = 9 animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: In P9-11 mice, significantly higher amounts of cell death are detected in layer V than in more superficial layers.
claims.source: But, whereas apoptosis similarly affects all layers in P1-3 mice (layer p=0.08), significantly higher amounts of cell death are detected in layer V than in more superficial layers of older P9-11 mice (layer p<0.0001, post-hoc test sectors b and c < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of quantitative data.

claims.claim: Spontaneous electrical activity is much more abundant and complex in S1 than in M1.
claims.source: Interestingly, previous in vivo recordings of the developing neocortex demonstrated that spontaneous electricalactivity is much more abundant and complex in S1 (Yang et al., 2009; An et al., 2014) than in M1 (Yang et al., 2009; An et al., 2014; Khazipov et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claims.claim: S1 activity is characterized by a significantly higher spectral power in the delta to gamma range than M1 activity in urethane-anesthetized mice.
claims.source: Comparative analysis of the in vivo network activity recorded in the two cortical areas demonstrates that S1 activity is characterized by a significantly higher spectral power in the delta to gamma range than M1 activity (Figure 4D1 and D2 and Figure 4—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, cortical area p<0.0001; frequency p<0.0001; n = 5 animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings and spectral analysis shown in Figure 4D with statistical testing.

claims.claim: In S1, the overall number of troughs (156 ± 27.8 min−1) is significantly higher than in M1 (63 ± 20 min−1) in urethane-anesthetized mice.
claims.source: A detailed analysis of this activity further reveals that in S1, the overall number of troughs (Figure 4D3 and Figure 4—source data 1; 156 ± 27.8 min−1, n = 5 animals) and the median trough frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 1.43 Hz, n = 2333 events) is significantly higher than the overall number of troughs (63 ± 20 min−1; Mann Whitney test, p=0.0317) and median trough frequency (0.82 Hz; n = 944 events; Mann Whitney test, p<0.001) in M1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4D3 with statistical testing.

claims.claim: In non-anesthetized animals, the spectral power of S1 in vivo activity is significantly higher than the spectral power of M1 in vivo activity.
claims.source: Also under this condition, the spectral power of S1 in vivo activity is significantly higher than the spectral power of M1 in vivo activity (Figure 4E1 and E2 and Figure 4—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, cortical area p=0.0015, n = 5 animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings in non-anesthetized animals shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In non-anesthetized animals, the trough rate in S1 (159.7 ± 23.6 min−1) is significantly higher than the trough rate in M1 (51.9 ± 23.4 min−1).
claims.source: Furthermore, the trough rate in S1 (Figure 4E3 and Figure 4—source data 2; 159.7 ± 23.6 min−1) is significantly higher than the trough rate in M1 (51.9 ± 23.4 min−1; Mann Whitney test p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of in vivo recordings in non-anesthetized animals shown in Figure 4E3 with statistical testing.

claims.claim: In vitro slices display a pattern of neuronal apoptosis similar to the in vivo situation with a high cell death density in cortical layers I-IV in M1 and significantly sparser aCasp3-positive neurons in the more lateral S1 sectors.
claims.source: Subsequent immunhistochemical analysis revealed that these in vitro slices display a pattern of neuronal apoptosis similar to the in vivo situation – that is with a high cell death density in cortical layers I-IV in M1 and significantly sparser aCasp3-positive neurons in the more lateral S1 sectors (Figure 5A2 and A3; one-way ANOVA, R²=0.34, p<0.0001, n = 7 hemispheres from seven animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of in vitro slices shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The overall rate of cell death in vitro is increased by about 4-fold compared to the in vivo situation.
claims.source: But in comparison to the in vivo situation, the overall rate of cell death is increased by about 4-fold (in vivo: 34.39 ± 14.44 aCasp3/mm²; in vitro: 132.67 + 39.2 aCasp3/mm², t-test = 0.040).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Bath application of 4-AP/0 Mg2+ ACSF results in significantly lower numbers of apoptotic neurons compared to untreated slices.
claims.source: Subsequent analysis of these slices shows significantly lower numbers of apoptotic neurons compared to untreated slices (Figure 5A3 and Figure 5—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, electrical activity p<0.0001, n = 6 slices from six animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A3 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: At 3 hr following dissection, rates of apoptosis are already decreased in slices exposed to 4-AP/0 Mg2+ for two hours compared to control conditions.
claims.source: At this earlier time point, rates of apoptosis are already decreased in slices exposed to 4-AP/0 Mg2+ for two hours compared to control conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; two-way ANOVA, sector p=0.001, electrical activity p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Disinhibition-induced activity by perfusing slices with 3 µM gabazine in low Mg2+ conditions results in a strong reduction in the rate of apoptosis in comparison to untreated control slices.
claims.source: The elevated levels of activity induced by this second pharmacological model likewise result in a strong reduction in the rate of apoptosis in comparison to untreated control slices (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, sector p=0.009, electrical activity p=0.001, n = 6 untreated hemispheres from six animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The density of apoptotic cells in adult (P27) cortical neurons is very low in comparison to P5-7 mice.
claims.source: Additional control experiments to investigate whether these effects are restricted to early developmental stages demonstrate that the density of apoptotic cells in adult (P27) cortical neurons is very low in comparison to P5-7 mice (Figure 5A3 and Figure 5—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, age p<0.0001, n = 6 hemispheres from three animals)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A3 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In adult cortical slices, apoptotic cells are homogenously distributed throughout all cortical areas analyzed.
claims.source: and homogenously distributed throughout all cortical areas analyzed (sectors p=0.30).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of adult cortical slice data.

claims.claim: Interictal and ictal-like activity induced by 4-AP/0 Mg2+ treatment is not correlated to enhanced apoptotic rates in adult slices.
claims.source: Interictal and ictal-like activity induced by 4-AP/0 Mg2+ treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, n = 6 hemispheres from three animals) is not correlated to enhanced apoptotic rates in these slices (electrical activity p=0.27).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Organotypic neocortical slices cultivated from newborn mice typically display spontaneous recurrent waves of activity propagating over the whole cortex.
claims.source: Organotypic neocortical slices cultivated from newborn mice typically display spontaneous recurrent waves of activity propagating over the whole cortex (Conhaim et al., 2011; Heck et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Quantification of aCasp3-positive neurons in organotypic slices after 4 days in vitro does not reveal any significant difference in the rate of apoptosis between cortical sectors covering M1 and S1.
claims.source: In line with our hypothesis, quantification of aCasp3-positive neurons in layers I to IV after 4 days in vitro (corresponding to P5-7) does not reveal any significant difference in the rate of apoptosis between cortical sectors covering M1 and S1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; one-way ANOVA, sector p=0.74, R²=0.07, n = 7 slices from seven animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of organotypic cultures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Upon silencing of electrical network by 1 µM TTX in organotypic slices, the overall rate of apoptosis significantly increases.
claims.source: Upon silencing of electrical network by 1 µM TTX, the overall rate of apoptosis significantly increases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; two-way ANOVA, condition p=0.0001, n = 3 slices from three animals)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Replay of in vivo activity in layers V-VI of the motor cortex results in a significant reduction of aCasp3-expressing neurons in the stimulated hemisphere when compared to the unstimulated, contralateral hemisphere.
claims.source: As expected from our previous results, replay of in vivo activity in layers V-VI of the motor cortex results in a significant reduction of aCasp3-expressing neurons in the stimulated hemisphere when compared to the unstimulated, contralateral hemisphere (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, electrical activity p=0.0008, n = 6 slices from six animals).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Replay of S1 activity has a significantly higher pro-survival effect than replayed M1 activity.
claims.source: In line with our hypothesis, replay of S1 activity has a significantly higher pro-survival effect than replayed M1 activity (Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 2; two-way ANOVA, stimulation pattern p=0.03, area p=0.63).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: A single intraperitoneal injection of kainate (2 mg/kg) induces tonic seizures in P5-7 mice within about 40 min.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work in P6 rats (Puskarjov et al., 2015), a single intraperitoneal injection of kainate (2 mg/kg) induces tonic seizures in P5-7 mice within about 40 min.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Modifying electrical activity levels in vivo affects the susceptibility of immature neurons to undergo apoptosis.
claims.source: Quantification of apoptosis in M1 and S1 regions of kainate- versus saline-injected mice demonstrates that also in vivo, modifying electrical activity levels affects the susceptibility of immature neurons to undergo apoptosis (Figure 7A and Figure 7—source data 1; two-way ANOVA, sector p<0.0001, condition p=0.005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In the somatosensory cortex, rates of apoptosis are not significantly reduced upon induction of epileptiform activity by kainate.
claims.source: Whereas in the somatosensory cortex, rates of apoptosis are not significantly reduced upon induction of epileptiform activity (control: 14.09 ± 2.49 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 7 mice; kainate: 9.28 ± 1.57 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 9 mice, post-hoc test p>0.05)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Levels of apoptosis in the primary motor cortex are significantly lower in kainate-injected mice (30.25 ± 6.16 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) than in saline-injected mice (52.03 ± 6.00 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²).
claims.source: levels of apoptosis in the primary motor cortex are significantly lower in kainate-injected mice (30.25 ± 6.16 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) than in saline-injected mice (52.03 ± 6.00 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², post-hoc test p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: A substantial portion of electrical activity in S1 is generated in the sensory periphery.
claims.source: A substantial portion of electrical activity in S1 is generated in the sensory periphery (Yang et al., 2009; Minlebaev et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Whisker deafferentation leads to an increased density of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding contralateral barrel field (18.74 ± 1.88 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²) as compared to the somatosensory cortex of the ipsilateral hemisphere receiving non-obstructed whisker afferents (13.77 ± 1.41 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²).
claims.source: Quantification of aCasp3-labeled cells shows that already within 5 hr, whisker deafferentation leads to an increased density of apoptotic neurons in the corresponding contralateral barrel field (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 2; 18.74 ± 1.88 aCasp3 positive cells/mm², n = 10 mice) as compared to the somatosensory cortex of the ipsilateral hemisphere receiving non-obstructed whisker afferents (13.77 ± 1.41 aCasp3 positive cells/mm²; t-test, p=0.038).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Electrical activity regulates cell death in the developing cortex in a cortical area-dependent manner.
claims.source: In summary, our data show for the first time that electrical activity regulates cell death in the developing cortex in a cortical area-dependent manner and thus represents an important factor for the functional and structural maturation of the brain.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: A mediolateral apoptosis profile of neocortical neurons comparable to the M1 versus S1 difference has been shown previously.
claims.source: While a mediolateral apoptosis profile of neocortical neurons comparable to the M1 versus S1 difference reported in the present study has been shown previously (Ikonomidou et al., 1999; Verney et al., 2000; Mosley et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A direct relation of apoptotic densities to functional neocortical areas has not been reported before this study.
claims.source: a direct relation of apoptotic densities to functional neocortical areas has, to our knowledge, not been reported before.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claims.claim: Neocortical slices reveal a higher number of apoptotic neurons compared to the same neocortical areas in vivo, possibly due to the lower rate of spontaneous electrical activity in acute slice preparations.
claims.source: Interestingly, neocortical slices reveal a higher number of apoptotic neurons compared to the same neocortical areas in vivo. This observation could be due to the lower rate of spontaneous electrical activity in acute slice preparations.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data and the hypothesis of the study.

claims.claim: The effect of kainate on reducing apoptosis is only significant for M1, but not for S1, either because the smaller number of apoptotic neurons in S1 impedes the analysis or because differences in electrical activity between S1 and M1 influence the amount of additional spikes introduced by convulsive conditions.
claims.source: This effect is only significant for M1, but not for S1, either because the smaller number of apoptotic neurons in S1 impedes the analysis of such rescue experiments, or because differences in the electrical activity between S1 and M1 influence the amount of additional spikes introduced by convulsive conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The survival of cortical neurons in silenced organotypic cultures is not due to an alternative pro-survival pathway but rather to the presence of pro-survival factors present within the culture medium.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesize that the survival of cortical neurons in silenced organotypic cultures is not due to an alternative pro-survival pathway but rather to the presence of pro-survival factors present within the culture medium.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claims.claim: Layers II to IV show more apoptotic neurons than layers V and VI in the first postnatal week.
claims.source: This finding is in line with a previous report demonstrating that layers II to IV show more apoptotic neurons than layers V and VI in the first postnatal week (Heumann and Leuba, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In vivo recordings in the M1 region of P6 mice across all neocortical layers do not show a negative correlation between activity levels and rates of apoptosis.
claims.source: Surprisingly, in vivo recordings in the M1 region of P6 mice across all neocortical layers do not show a negative correlation between activity levels and rates of apoptosis (unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claims.claim: Lower layer VI contains the early-generated subplate neurons.
claims.source: Lower layer VI contains the early-generated subplate neurons (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013; Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Higashi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A proportion of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis during the first postnatal weeks.
claims.source: It has been suggested that a proportion of these neurons is eliminated by apoptosis during the first postnatal weeks (Price et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The low cell death density in layer VI is attributed to the subplate layer being very thin (about 50 µm-width) and apoptotic neurons being cleared away by macrophages within 2.5 hr.
claims.source: We attribute this low cell death density to two reasons. First, the subplate layer represents a very thin layer of about 50 µm-width located between the white matter and layer VI-a (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013). Because, apoptotic neurons are cleared away by macrophages with 2.5 hr (Thomaidou et al., 1997), the chance to stain apoptotic neurons in this layer is very low.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on anatomical knowledge and a citation about macrophage clearance.

claims.claim: Only a fraction of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis, while other subplate neurons such as Nurr1 or Lpar1-GFP-labeled neurons survive beyond the postnatal period.
claims.source: Second, recent reports have demonstrated that only a fraction of subplate neurons is eliminated by apoptosis, while other subplate neurons such as Nurr1 or Lpar1-GFP-labeled neurons survive beyond the postnatal period (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The layer VI-b consists of persistent neurons from the subplate layer.
claims.source: In line with the existence of a substantial fraction of surviving subplate neurons, it has been recently shown that the layer VI-b consists of persistent neurons from the subplate layer (Marx et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: In the immature brain, including that of humans, a variety of intrinsically-generated and sensory-evoked activity patterns can be observed in different cortical areas.
claims.source: In the immature brain, including that of humans, a variety of intrinsically-generated and sensory-evoked activity patterns can be observed in different cortical areas (An et al., 2014; Milh et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2009; Khazipov et al., 2004; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Kilb et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The distinct levels of spontaneous neuronal activity in the immature sensory, motor or association cortex have been frequently attributed to the development of adequate connectivity.
claims.source: The distinct levels of spontaneous neuronal activity in the immature sensory, motor or association cortex have been frequently attributed to the development of adequate connectivity (Chen and Ghosh, 2005; Luhmann et al., 2016; Spitzer, 2012; Hartung et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Human brains display activity patterns similar to the rodent ones.
claims.source: Human brains display activity patterns similar to the rodent ones (Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006; Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006).

results.result: The study characterizes the temporal and spatial pattern of developmental apoptosis in the mouse neocortex. Cell death peaks at P5-7, predominantly affects glutamatergic neurons in superficial layers (I-IV), and shows striking area-specific differences with M1 exhibiting 4-fold higher apoptosis than S1 in layers I-IV, while layer V shows the opposite pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C28 provide comprehensive characterization of apoptosis patterns with quantitative data, statistical analysis, and validation using both aCasp3 and TUNEL staining (C26). The temporal profile (C16, C27, C28), layer-specific differences (C22, C24, C25), and area-specific differences (C23) are all supported by rigorous quantification and appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: In vivo electrophysiological recordings demonstrate that S1 exhibits significantly higher spontaneous electrical activity than M1, as measured by spectral power across delta to gamma frequencies and trough frequency, in both urethane-anesthetized and non-anesthetized P6-7 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 and C85 are supported by simultaneous in vivo recordings from both cortical areas with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA). The findings are validated in both anesthetized and non-anesthetized conditions (C32, C33), strengthening the conclusion that activity differences are not artifacts of anesthesia.

results.result: The rate of apoptosis in M1 versus S1 negatively correlates with region-dependent levels of spontaneous electrical activity, with S1 showing higher activity and lower apoptosis than M1.
results.evaluation: The correlation between activity levels (C29-C33) and apoptosis rates (C3) is supported by quantitative measurements from both in vivo recordings and immunohistochemical analysis. The negative correlation is demonstrated across multiple measures of activity (spectral power, trough frequency) and is consistent in both anesthetized and non-anesthetized conditions.

results.result: Pharmacologically increasing electrical activity in acute cortical slices using 4-AP/0 Mg2+ or gabazine/0 Mg2+ significantly reduces apoptosis rates within 2-4 hours, while preserving the area-specific pattern observed in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by in vitro experiments with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. Two independent pharmacological approaches (C36, C38) produce consistent results, and the time course is established (C37). The preservation of area-specific patterns in vitro (C34) validates the model, though overall apoptosis is elevated 4-fold compared to in vivo (C35).

results.result: The pro-survival effect of increased electrical activity is specific to immature cortical networks, as adult (P27) cortical slices show low, homogeneous apoptosis that is insensitive to activity manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C89 demonstrate age-specificity through direct comparison of P5-7 and P27 slices with statistical analysis. The lack of response to 4-AP/0 Mg2+ in adult slices (C41) and the homogeneous distribution of apoptosis (C40) provide strong evidence that activity-dependent apoptosis regulation is developmentally restricted.

results.result: In organotypic cultures where electrical activity is synchronized across the cortex, regional differences in apoptosis are abolished, and silencing activity with TTX increases overall apoptosis, demonstrating that activity-dependent processes underlie area-specific apoptosis patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 and C90-C91 provide strong evidence through organotypic culture experiments. The abolishment of regional differences in the presence of synchronized activity (C43, C90) and the increase in apoptosis upon TTX treatment (C44, C91) support the causal role of electrical activity. However, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about why TTX doesn't reveal regional differences (C112).

results.result: Electrical replay of in vivo S1 activity patterns to M1 in vitro produces a significantly stronger pro-survival effect than replay of M1 activity patterns, providing direct evidence that activity pattern differences causally determine area-specific apoptosis rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 and C94-C96 demonstrate causality through a sophisticated experimental design where in vivo activity patterns are replayed in vitro. The stimulation protocols accurately reproduce temporal distributions of in vivo events (C95), and the differential effects of S1 versus M1 patterns (C46) provide strong causal evidence. Statistical analysis supports the conclusions (two-way ANOVA, p=0.03 for stimulation pattern).

results.result: In vivo induction of epileptiform activity by kainate injection significantly reduces apoptosis in M1 but not in S1, demonstrating that elevated activity can rescue neurons from apoptosis in vivo, particularly in areas with physiologically low activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 and C97 are supported by in vivo kainate experiments with appropriate controls (saline injection). The area-specific effect (significant in M1 but not S1, C49-C50) is consistent with the hypothesis. However, the authors acknowledge alternative explanations for the lack of effect in S1 (C57), including potential floor effects or differential responses to kainate.

results.result: Unilateral whisker deafferentation for 5 hours leads to increased apoptosis in the corresponding contralateral S1 barrel field compared to the ipsilateral hemisphere, demonstrating that periphery-driven activity provides anti-apoptotic signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C98 are supported by sensory deprivation experiments with within-animal controls (contralateral vs ipsilateral comparison). The 5-hour time window is relatively short, strengthening the causal interpretation. Statistical significance is achieved (t-test, p=0.038), though the effect size is modest (18.74 vs 13.77 aCasp3+ cells/mm²).

results.result: Electrical activity is a major determinant of region-dependent apoptosis rates in the developing neocortex and represents an important factor for functional and structural brain maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C99, C102, and C110 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: correlation studies (in vivo recordings), pharmacological manipulations (in vitro and in vivo), activity replay experiments, and sensory deprivation. The consistency across different experimental paradigms provides strong support for these conclusions.

results.result: aCasp3 is validated as a reliable marker for detecting apoptotic neurons at various stages of degradation, as confirmed by concordance with TUNEL staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C78-C80 establish the validity of the primary detection method. The comparison between aCasp3 and TUNEL (C26) shows no significant difference in detection method (two-way ANOVA, p=0.96), validating aCasp3 as reliable. The citations support the characterization of aCasp3 as an early marker (C78) and TUNEL as a late marker (C79).

results.result: In flat-mounted sections, M1 shows higher densities of aCasp3-positive cells than S1, with most apoptotic neurons located in layer II at the border of layer I, and aCasp3 labeling detects neurons at various stages of degradation.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 reports a trend (M1: 39.66±14.93 vs S1: 15.51±6.90 aCasp3/mm²) but explicitly states it is not statistically significant (p=0.28, n=3). While C20-C21 are supported by microscopy data, the lack of statistical significance for the primary comparison and small sample size (n=3) make this result uncertain. The authors subsequently use coronal sections for quantitative analysis.

results.result: In vitro slices show 4-fold higher apoptosis than in vivo, possibly due to lower spontaneous activity, and the differential effect of kainate between M1 and S1 may reflect floor effects or activity-dependent differences in response to convulsive conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are speculative interpretations (C56, C57) or hypotheses (C58) proposed by the authors to explain their observations. While the 4-fold increase in vitro is documented (C35), the mechanistic explanations are not directly tested. These represent reasonable hypotheses but lack experimental validation.

results.result: Layer-specific patterns of apoptosis do not consistently correlate with activity levels across all layers, as in vivo recordings in M1 across layers do not show negative correlation with apoptosis rates.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is based on unpublished data and contradicts the general hypothesis. While C59 is supported by citation, the lack of correlation in M1 across layers (C60) suggests additional factors beyond activity levels may regulate layer-specific apoptosis. The authors acknowledge this complexity but do not resolve it.

results.result: The low apoptosis density in layer VI is attributed to the thin subplate layer, rapid clearance by macrophages, and the fact that only a fraction of subplate neurons undergo apoptosis while others persist as layer VI-b.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 provide a comprehensive explanation for low layer VI apoptosis, supported by citations to anatomical studies (C61, C64, C65) and macrophage clearance kinetics (C63). The interpretation is consistent with current understanding of subplate neuron fate, though the authors' specific observations are limited.

results.result: Background on developmental apoptosis: programmed cell death affects up to 50% of neurons in rodents through two waves (embryonic and postnatal), mediated by the mitochondrial pathway and Bcl-2 family proteins, with activity-dependent regulation in the CNS differing from the neurotrophic theory of the PNS.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C6-C15 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These establish the context for the current study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is accurate.

results.result: Immature brains, including human preterm infants, display diverse intrinsically-generated and sensory-evoked activity patterns across cortical areas, with human delta brushes resembling rodent spindle bursts.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 establish the translational relevance of the findings by citing studies of activity patterns in developing human brains. The citations support the similarity between rodent and human developmental activity patterns, providing context for the clinical implications discussed later.

results.result: Alterations in neuronal number due to modified apoptosis may contribute to neuropsychiatric disorders including autism spectrum disorders, which show elevated neuronal numbers, and sensory deprivation during development causes behavioral deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 discuss clinical implications supported by citations to prior studies. C73 is a proposal by the authors suggesting activity-dependent apoptosis as a mechanism for autism-related neuronal excess, complementing the neurogenesis hypothesis (C72). This is a reasonable speculation based on their findings but not directly tested.

results.result: The study's findings have broad implications: neuronal activity influences apoptosis in addition to other developmental processes, physiological activity patterns are essential for circuit development, and disruptions may contribute to neuropsychiatric diseases in both rodents and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 and C99, C115-C117 represent the broader implications and conclusions of the study. These are supported by the experimental findings and appropriate citations to related work. C116-C117 involve extrapolation to humans based on similarity of activity patterns (C68-C69), which is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: The study extends previous observations of mediolateral apoptosis gradients by demonstrating, for the first time, a direct relation between apoptotic densities and functional cortical areas, which cannot be explained by differential maturation but likely reflects area-dependent intrinsic properties or pro-survival signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C81-C82, C103-C105 establish the novelty and significance of the findings. The claim of novelty (C55) is supported by appropriate citations to prior work showing gradients (C54) but not functional area specificity. The exclusion of maturation differences (C81) is supported by citation, and the proposed mechanisms (C82) are reasonable hypotheses.

results.result: The study confirms and extends prior in vitro findings by demonstrating that elevated activity reduces apoptosis in both in vitro and in vivo conditions, with effects detectable within 2 hours, which has clinical relevance given the susceptibility of immature brains to activity changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 and C106-C109 connect the current findings to prior in vitro work and establish the rapid time course of effects. The confirmation in vivo (C107) and the 2-hour time window (C108) are novel contributions. The clinical relevance (C109) is supported by citation to prior work on immature brain susceptibility.

results.result: Organotypic culture experiments suggest that electrical activity per se provides the major regionalization cue for apoptosis, with elevated activity producing rapid effects (4 hours) while chronic blockade has more moderate effects, though complete absence of synaptic transmission causes dramatic apoptosis in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 involve interpretation of organotypic culture results, with C112 being explicitly speculative ('tempting to postulate'). The asymmetry between activity elevation and blockade effects (C113) is observed but not fully explained. C114 is supported by citation but the relationship to the current findings is unclear. The interpretation requires additional validation.

results.result: Apoptosis and early spontaneous activity are phylogenetically conserved features of immature cortical networks that may mutually interact to ensure proper cortical development.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 provide the conceptual framework for the study. C100 is supported by citations to prior work on evolutionary conservation. C101 is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that is subsequently tested and supported by their experimental findings. This represents the key conceptual advance of the study.
